Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in how they treat history.

**`git merge`** ties the two branches together with a new merge commit that has two parents. Existing commits are untouched.

```
A---B---C---F---G  main
     \           \
      D---E-------M  feature   (git merge main, run on feature)
```

**`git rebase`** replays your commits one by one on top of the other branch, creating new commits with new hashes. The result is a straight line, as if you had started your work from the latest tip.

```
A---B---C---F---G  main
                 \
                  D'---E'  feature   (git rebase main, run on feature)
```

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserved exactly, with branch points and merge commits | Rewritten into a linear sequence |
| Commit hashes | Unchanged | New for every replayed commit |
| Conflicts | Resolved once, in the merge commit | Resolved per replayed commit, possibly several times |
| Shared branches | Safe | Risky, because others' copies no longer match |
| Undoing | Revert the merge commit | Recover the old tip via `git reflog` |

**When to use which**

- **Rebase** to tidy up a local or personal feature branch before sharing it, or to bring it up to date with `main` without cluttering it with merge commits.
- **Merge** to bring a finished feature into a shared branch, or whenever the branch is one that others have pulled.

The main rule is not to rebase commits that other people have based work on. Because rebase replaces those commits with new ones, collaborators end up with diverged history, and you would need to force push (`git push --force-with-lease`) to update the remote.

A common workflow combines both: rebase your feature branch onto `main` locally to get a clean series of commits, then merge it into `main`.
